source: Anchored to public NASA figures where a real unit exists: VIPER rover fact sheet and instrument pages (NSS, NIRVSS, MSolo, TRIDENT; 430 kg rover, 450 W peak solar, 0.72 km/h), the MMRTG fact sheet (about 110 W electric and 2,000 W thermal at launch, 45 kg, plutonium-238 half-life 87.7 years), the NASA Small Spacecraft Technology State-of-the-Art report (solar cell efficiency, battery specific energy, radios, avionics) and NASA flight computer descriptions (RAD750, HPSC). Masses, powers and costs of generic parts are representative values for their class, rounded for gameplay.
units: mass_kg dry mass; power_w electrical draw while the part is on; cost_musd millions of US dollars; trl NASA technology readiness level 1-9; failure_rate_per_year chance of a disabling fault per year of operation; data_rate_mbps megabits per second averaged over the time the instrument operates (compressed products, not the raw detector rate); max_rate_mbps the ceiling of the radio hardware.

parts.name: Light composite frame
parts.summary: Saves mass on every burn, but carries only a lean set of equipment.

parts.name: Standard aluminium frame
parts.summary: Flight-proven structure with room for a full science payload.

parts.name: Heavy-duty frame
parts.summary: Carries anything in the catalog. Every extra kilogram of frame costs more than a kilogram of propellant to land.

parts.name: Body-mounted solar deck, 2 m²
parts.summary: Cells on the top deck: light, cheap and nothing to deploy. They face the sky, so they only work well where the Sun climbs high.

parts.name: Vertical side panels, 3 × 1 m²
parts.summary: Panels on three sides, like VIPER: whichever way the vehicle turns, one of them faces a Sun that sits on the horizon.

parts.name: Sun-tracking mast array, 6 m²
parts.summary: A tall array that turns to follow the Sun: several times the power, and a new mechanism that has never flown and may slip the schedule.

parts.name: Radioisotope generator (MMRTG)
parts.summary: Plutonium heat turned into about 110 W, day and night, sunlit or not, and its waste heat keeps the vehicle warm. Low power, high price.

parts.name: Lithium-ion battery, 2 kWh
parts.summary: Enough for short dips into shadow. A long night empties it.

parts.name: Lithium-ion battery, 6 kWh
parts.summary: About two days of work in the dark, close to what VIPER carries.

parts.name: Lithium-ion battery, 15 kWh
parts.summary: Big enough to hibernate through a two-week lunar night, at the mass of a whole instrument suite.

parts.name: Hydrazine monopropellant stage
parts.summary: One propellant, few valves, very reliable. Its low exhaust speed means far more propellant for the same manoeuvres.

parts.name: Storable bipropellant stage
parts.summary: Fuel and oxidiser that stay liquid for years. The standard choice for landers: good efficiency, proven hardware.

parts.name: Methane-oxygen stage
parts.summary: The most efficient engine here, with thrust to spare. Its cold propellants boil away in a couple of weeks, so it cannot take the slow route.

parts.name: Sun sensors and gyros
parts.summary: Knows roughly which way is up. Good enough for wide antennas, not for a narrow beam.

parts.name: Star tracker and reaction wheels
parts.summary: Precise pointing: needed to keep a high-gain dish on Earth and to aim narrow instruments.

parts.name: Commercial-grade computer
parts.summary: Fast, light and cheap. A burst of solar radiation can crash it and cost you days.

parts.name: Radiation-hardened computer (RAD750 class)
parts.summary: The processor family that flies on NASA's Mars rovers: slow, with little storage, and it shrugs off solar storms.

parts.name: High-performance spaceflight computer
parts.summary: Hardened and powerful enough to drive and drill without waiting for Earth. New hardware: more cost, more schedule risk.

parts.name: S-band low-gain radio
parts.summary: Talks in every direction at once, slowly. Commands and health data get through; pictures queue up.

parts.name: X-band medium-gain antenna
parts.summary: A wider beam that is easy to keep on Earth, with a useful data rate.

parts.name: X-band steerable high-gain dish
parts.summary: Ten times the data rate through a narrow beam. It needs precise pointing and a clear view of Earth.

parts.name: Lunar relay service link
parts.summary: Pays for passes of a relay satellite in lunar orbit: contact even where Earth is below the horizon, for the price of a subscription.

parts.name: Blankets and radiators
parts.summary: Passive insulation. In shadow the heaters must replace all the heat that leaks out.

parts.name: Warm box with louvers and heat switches
parts.summary: Closes itself up in the cold, cutting heater power by about 40 %.

parts.name: Warm box with radioisotope heater units
parts.summary: Small plutonium pellets give free heat for decades. They make a lunar night survivable, and they need nuclear launch approval and money.

parts.name: Four-wheel rover chassis
parts.summary: Simple fixed suspension. It drives on gentle ground only and slowly.

parts.name: Four-wheel steering with active suspension
parts.summary: Every wheel steers and lifts on its own, like VIPER: twice the speed, crater slopes within reach, more mass and power.

parts.name: Radar altimeter landing
parts.summary: Knows its height, not what is underneath. It lands kilometres off target, and polar terrain is full of boulders and long shadows.

parts.name: Terrain-relative navigation
parts.summary: Matches camera images to an onboard map, the method that put Perseverance down within metres of its target.

parts.name: Navigation with hazard-detection lidar
parts.summary: Scans the ground in the last seconds and diverts around rocks. The safest landing; the divert costs propellant and the sensor is new.

parts.name: Neutron spectrometer
parts.summary: Senses hydrogen, the signature of water, up to a metre underground while the rover drives. Tiny, frugal and essential for finding where to drill.

parts.name: Near-infrared spectrometer
parts.summary: Reads the colour of the surface and of drill cuttings to tell water ice from dry minerals.

parts.name: Mass spectrometer
parts.summary: Weighs the gas molecules released by drilling: the proof of what the ice is made of. It needs a drill to feed it.

parts.name: One-metre percussive drill
parts.summary: Brings up cuttings from a metre down, as far as VIPER reaches. Power-hungry while it runs.

parts.name: Two-metre deep drill
parts.summary: Twice the depth, where older ice may lie. Heavy, hungry and unproven: it can jam and it can slip the schedule.

parts.name: Stereo science cameras
parts.summary: Colour panoramas and 3D terrain. Images are the bulkiest data aboard and will fill the recorder unless the downlink keeps up.

parts.name: Ground-penetrating radar
parts.summary: Profiles buried layers along the drive, showing how deep the ice-bearing ground goes.

parts.name: Thermal infrared radiometer
parts.summary: Maps ground temperature to find the cold traps where ice can last for billions of years.
